claim: *Intervention boundaries.* Guidance influences reasoning; enforcement constrains actions or determines whether work and artifacts are accepted. Moving from individual actions to larger units of work can make additional obligations legible as evidence accumulates. Later boundaries are not necessarily stronger. Choose the earliest boundary where the obligation can be evaluated and enforced.
topology: The only arrow is the straight rightward scope axis below the cards. It denotes increasing scope and additional evaluation context, not enforcement strength. A vertical divider and a separate enclosure distinguish guidance from enforcement.
required_terms: Task-completion checks merge gates deployment gates
bw_encoding: Only the enforcement-boundaries enclosure uses light 5% gray. All four cards remain white; no tone implies increasing enforcement strength. Group headings are bold 11 pt; boundary names are bold 10 pt. Row labels and scope-arrow annotations are plain italic 10 pt. Scope descriptions and examples are regular 10 pt.
redesign: Author-requested four-column comparison of reasoning input, action, work unit and artifact/runtime. Boundary, Scope and Examples become aligned rows; reasoning input remains guidance outside the enforcement enclosure.
alt: Four columns compare intervention boundaries. Reasoning input is guidance: context supplied to the reasoner, with instructions, models and examples. The three enforcement boundaries are action, covering one proposed action with permissions, hooks and tool restrictions; work unit, covering a composed body of work with task-completion checks, merge gates and deployment gates; and artifact or runtime, covering the resulting artifact or running state with API boundaries, schemas and runtime permissions. Rows identify Boundary, Scope and Examples. A rightward arrow indicates increasing scope of work considered and more context for evaluating obligations, not increasing enforcement strength.
